body.head: An Indian Bureau Reminiscence
body.p:
AtAfter the close of the Secession war in '65 I worked for several months, (until Mr. Harlan turned me out for writing "Leaves of Grass,") in the Interior Department at Washington, in the Indian Bureau. Along this time ‸there came to Washington to see their Great Father, an unusual number of Indianaboriginal visitors delegations for treaties, settlement of lands,‸&c.,—
groups of —some young and middle aged, and somebut mainly old men, from the West, North, and occasionally from the South—‸—several hundreds of them, in parties of from twenty the most wonderful proofs of what Nature can produce,
(the survival of the fittest, no doubt, and theall the frailer samples, ‸drop, sorted out, by death)—‸—as if to showhow the earth and woods the attrition of storms and elements ‸and the exigencies of life at first hand can train and fashion men, and what they can turn out indeed chiefs, men

(A wise man called "the Flesh" ‸now makes a short speech, apparently asking something. Indian Commissioner Dole is answeringanswers him and the interpreter translates in scraps again.) All the ‸principal chiefs have tomahawks or hatchets, some of them very richly ornamented and costly. Plaid shirts are to be observed—none too clean. Now a tall fellow
"Hole-in-the-Day," is speaking. He has a copious head⹀dress ‸composed of feathers and narrow ribbon, under which appears a countenance painted all over a bilious yellow. Let us note this young chief, ‸however, For all his paint, "Hole-in-the-Day" is a handsome Indian, very gentlemanly, mild and calm, dressed in black drab buckskin leggings, and a drabdark gray surtout, ‸and a soft black hat. His costume is perfectwill, ‸bear full observation, and even fashion would accept him.

His apparel is worn loose and scant enough to show a‸his superb physique, especially in neck, chest and legs. (The
‸Apollo Belvidere!" was the involuntary exclamation of a famous European artist when he first saw a good specimen of a ‸full⹀grownyoung Choc Choctaw.)
